say.text: A 32-year-old man has had right lower abdominal pain for 14 hours. CT shows uncomplicated appendicitis with no appendicolith.
He is fit and understands that some patients need surgery later. Which statement is right?

choices.label: Appendicectomy is the only treatment, so surgery cannot be avoided
Antibiotics-first is an accepted option for selected patients like him
Antibiotics-first is the right choice for every patient with appendicitis
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Check each option against the stem: CT-proven, uncomplicated, no appendicolith, and a patient who accepts a later operation if needed.
Yes. Past papers expected 'appendicectomy is the only treatment'. Current practice accepts antibiotics-first for selected, CT-proven, uncomplicated adults.
Keep the conditions with the headline: they decide who qualifies.
Tempting if you learned 'treatment of choice' as 'only treatment'. Re-read the stem: what kind of disease does this man have, and what does the CT add?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look twice: 'treatment of choice' and 'only treatment' are not the same claim.

say.text: Appendicectomy is the treatment of choice, and past papers expected it as the only treatment. Current practice accepts antibiotics-first for selected adults with CT-proven uncomplicated appendicitis.
Tempting as an over-correction. Which words in the stem set this patient apart from other appendicitis patients?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look twice: the option is accepted only with conditions attached.

say.text: Antibiotics-first is for selected adults with CT-proven uncomplicated appendicitis. A significant proportion later need appendicectomy, and an appendicolith predicts failure.
A 34-year-old has CT-proven appendicitis with no perforation or abscess. The CT also shows an appendicolith.
He asks about antibiotics alone. What is the best management?

choices.label: Appendicectomy, since this CT finding predicts antibiotic failure
Antibiotics alone, since the CT shows no perforation or abscess
The Ochsner-Sherren regimen, as for an appendicular mass
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Qualifiers matter. Antibiotics-first needs three things at once: CT-proven, uncomplicated, and no appendicolith. Which does this man lack?
Yes. An appendicolith predicts failure of antibiotics-first and raises the risk of perforation.
So the three conditions are CT-proven, uncomplicated, and no appendicolith.
Tempting, because the disease is not yet complicated. But uncomplicated is only one of the conditions. Check what else the CT reports.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look twice: one CT finding changes who is a candidate.

say.text: Antibiotics-first needs CT-proven uncomplicated disease. An appendicolith predicts failure of antibiotics and carries a higher risk of perforation, so he goes to appendicectomy.
Tempting because it is a conservative plan you know. Ask what that regimen is for: a mass, or an inflamed appendix with no mass?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look twice: the regimen is tied to a lump, not to an appendicolith.

say.text: The Ochsner-Sherren regimen treats an appendicular mass. This man has no mass, and the appendicolith points to surgery, not a conservative regimen.
A 24-year-old has had five days of right iliac fossa pain. He is stable with a low-grade fever and a tender, palpable mass in the right iliac fossa.
What is the next step?

choices.label: Emergency appendicectomy through a gridiron incision
Laparotomy and open drainage of the mass
Conservative treatment by the Ochsner-Sherren regimen
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The words that matter are 'five days', 'stable' and 'palpable mass'. Think about what the omentum has done by day five.
Yes. The regimen is nil by mouth or liquids, IV fluids, IV antibiotics, analgesia, and charting of pulse, temperature and mass size.
Tempting: appendicitis usually means operate. Re-read the stem: is this a mass that has been walled off, or a fresh inflamed appendix?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look twice: the mass changes the first step.

say.text: Omentum and bowel loops wall off the appendix into a mass. A stable patient with a mass is managed conservatively, by the Ochsner-Sherren regimen.
Open drainage belongs to an abscess, and only after image-guided drainage fails. Does the stem describe pus, or a mass?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look twice: a mass is not yet an abscess.

say.text: A mass is treated conservatively. Only an abscess is drained, usually percutaneously under imaging, and open drainage is kept for failure or unavailability.
The regimen is stopped and surgery done if the pulse rises, pain or mass size increases, peritonitis spreads, or vomiting starts.
The mass in a 55-year-old man has resolved on the regimen. He feels well.
What is the next step?

choices.label: Colonoscopy or CT to exclude caecal carcinoma, then selective interval surgery
Routine interval appendicectomy at 6-8 weeks, with no other work-up
Discharge now, with review only if symptoms come back
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Two things are in play: how old the patient is, and what an old caecal growth could look like after an appendiceal mass.
Yes. Past papers expected interval surgery at 6-8 weeks. Now it is selective, and colonoscopy or CT is advised in older patients, over about 40.
This is the keyed answer in many past papers, so it feels safe. Ask what current practice adds for an older patient.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look twice: the old key skips a check that age makes necessary.

say.text: Past papers expected interval appendicectomy at 6-8 weeks. Current practice is selective, with colonoscopy or CT in patients over about 40 to exclude caecal carcinoma.
This swings too far the other way. In an older patient, what could the mass have been hiding?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look twice: 'now selective' does not mean 'no work-up'.

say.text: Interval surgery is now selective, but the work-up is not optional in older patients: colonoscopy or CT is advised over about 40 to exclude caecal carcinoma.
A 30-year-old has a swinging fever after several days of right iliac fossa pain. Imaging shows a drainable appendicular collection.
What is the best treatment?

choices.label: Laparotomy and open drainage as the first step
Emergency appendicectomy to remove the source at once
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The stem says 'drainable collection'. Think of the least invasive route to a collection you can see on imaging.
Yes. Abscess means drain it, usually percutaneously with imaging. Open drainage is kept for failure or when this is not available.
Open drainage is a fallback, not the opening move. What can be done through the skin with imaging?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look twice: the order of steps is what is tested.

say.text: An appendicular abscess is drained, usually percutaneously under imaging with antibiotics. Open drainage is for failure or when imaging drainage is not available.
Tempting because the appendix is the source. But what has the body already done around it?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look twice: pus is already walled off.

say.text: The omentum and bowel have walled off the appendix and pus has formed an abscess. Drain it percutaneously with antibiotics first.
Which of these is NOT a complication of acute appendicitis itself, before any operation?

choices.label: Stump appendicitis from a long remnant
Pylephlebitis with rigors, jaundice and liver abscesses
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Sort the options by cause: from the inflamed appendix itself, or from the operation. Which one needs an appendix stump to exist?
Yes. Stump appendicitis comes from leaving a long stump, so it needs the operation first.
Disease complications: perforation with peritonitis, mass, abscess, pylephlebitis.
That one does arise from the disease. Ask for each option: does it need an operation to have happened first?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look twice: peritonitis follows perforation, with no knife involved.

say.text: Perforation with generalised peritonitis, appendicular mass, abscess and pylephlebitis are all complications of the disease itself.
It sounds like a surgical aftermath, but ask what produces it. Does it need an operation first?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look twice: this arises from the diseased appendix.

say.text: Pylephlebitis is septic thrombophlebitis of the portal venous system with rigors, jaundice and liver abscesses. It is a disease complication, not a surgical one.
What is the most common complication after appendicectomy?

choices.label: Faecal fistula from a slipped stump ligature
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about where the operation touches the patient most. Which complication happens at that site and also most often?
Yes. Wound infection is the most common complication after appendicectomy, and laparoscopy lowers it.
True as a complication, but rare. The question asks for the most common one. Think of the incision itself.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look twice: the key word is 'most common'.

say.text: Faecal fistula is a real surgical complication, but wound infection is the most common after appendicectomy.
Pylephlebitis arises from the disease, not the operation. Which complication comes from the wound?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look twice: you have drawn from the disease list.

say.text: Pylephlebitis is a complication of the disease. After the operation, the most common problem is wound infection.
After open appendicectomy through McBurney's point, a 28-year-old develops a right groin bulge and numbness over the groin.
Which nerve was injured?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The bulge and numbness are over the groin. Which nerve of the iliac region crosses the muscle-splitting incision and supplies that area?
Yes. A gridiron incision can injure the ilioinguinal nerve, which leads to a right inguinal hernia.
A close neighbour, and easy to mix up. Which nerve runs where the gridiron incision splits the muscles, and leads to an inguinal hernia?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look twice: the three iliac-region nerves are learned as a bundle, and this is the one that gets confused.

say.text: The right inguinal hernia after a gridiron incision comes from injury to the ilioinguinal nerve, not its neighbour.
The femoral nerve supplies the thigh, not the groin wall. Try again with the groin bulge in mind.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look twice: the incision lies over the muscle layers of the abdominal wall.

say.text: The gridiron incision splits oblique muscles along their fibres. Injury to the ilioinguinal nerve there weakens the groin and gives a right inguinal hernia.
Last check. An exam stem says 'treatment of choice for acute appendicitis'. A second stem says 'the only treatment'.
How do you answer each?

choices.label: Choice is appendicectomy; 'only' is the old key; antibiotics-first suits selected adults
Appendicectomy for both, since antibiotics have no accepted role
Antibiotics for both, since they have replaced appendicectomy as treatment of choice
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Separate the two phrases. One names the usual best treatment; the other claims there is no alternative at all.
Yes. Treatment of choice is appendicectomy, laparoscopic if available. 'Only treatment' was the older key; current practice accepts antibiotics-first for selected patients.
Reading both as the same claim is the old absolute. What does current practice allow for selected adults?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look twice: the word 'only' is the cue to an outdated absolute.

say.text: Treatment of choice is appendicectomy, now usually laparoscopic. Past papers expected 'only treatment'; current practice accepts antibiotics-first for selected CT-proven uncomplicated adults.
That swings too far. Appendicectomy is still the standard choice, and antibiotics-first has conditions attached.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look twice: antibiotics-first is an option for a subset, not a replacement.

say.text: Appendicectomy remains the treatment of choice. Antibiotics-first applies only to selected adults with CT-proven uncomplicated disease, and an appendicolith predicts failure.

cards.q: Who is a candidate for antibiotics-first in appendicitis?
cards.a: A selected adult with CT-proven uncomplicated disease and no appendicolith.
Conservative, by the Ochsner-Sherren regimen; stop and operate if pulse, pain or mass size rises or peritonitis spreads.

cards.q: Interval appendicectomy after a mass: old key and current view?
cards.a: Old key 6-8 weeks routinely; now selective, with colonoscopy or CT in patients over about 40.

cards.q: Best treatment for an appendicular abscess?
cards.a: Image-guided percutaneous drainage with antibiotics; open drainage if that fails.

cards.q: Most common complication after appendicectomy, and the nerve at risk with a gridiron incision?
cards.a: Wound infection; ilioinguinal nerve, giving a right inguinal hernia.
